newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenians vote in second poll since secession.
newsitem.headline: Slovenians vote in second poll since secession.

text.p: Slovenians voted on Sunday in their second general election since independence from Yugoslavia in 1991, with polls showing the ruling centre-left Liberal Democrats likely to win most votes.
The Alpine republic's 3,534 polling stations opened at 7 a.m. local time (0600 GMT) and were due to close at 1800 GMT when first computer projections of the results were expected.
About 1.5 million people were eligible to vote for the 24 political parties fielding a total of 1,300 candidates for the election to the 90-seat lower house of parliament.
The pro-Europe Liberal Democrats of Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek have headed a fractious coalition since the last nationwide poll in 1992.
But Drnovsek managed to hold his administration together to cement a stable democracy and marshal one of the most successful economies among Europe's former communist states.

Slovenia, bordered by Italy, Hungary, Austria and Croatia, has applied to join the European Union by the year 2001 and has a good chance of being included in the first wave of ex-communist states to join the NATO military alliance.
President Milan Kucan, the former Slovenian communist party chief who defied Belgrade's rule to lead his country to secession, was among the first to vote.
Kucan, speaking to reporters after casting his ballot near his modest home in the south of the capital, said voters would support those parties committed to securing a stable future.
"They will support parties which are not just interested in arguing and looking back to the past, but those who have something to offer other than empty promises," he said.
Voters turned out early to vote in Ljubljana on an overcast and dry day. Preliminary figures were not immediately available. In the 1992 election, a huge 85.8 percent of voters cast their ballot.
After a series of defections, the Liberal Democrats ruled most recently in coalition with the conservative Christian Democrats with support from independents.

The United List of Social Democrats, the former communists, quit the coalition in January following a row over Drnovsek's economic reforms aimed at capping inflation and public spending to put Slovenia on track for EU membership.
In 1994, the centre-right Social Democrats withdrew support when their leader Janez Jansa was sacked as defence minister.
Jansa had been hailed a hero of the independence struggle for organising military forces to combat Yugoslav federal troops in a 10-day war in June 1991, in which 64 people died.
Now one of Drnovsek's keenest rivals, Jansa has been instrumental in setting up a loose alliance of rightist parties to try to unseat the Liberal Democrats from power.
But polls showed combined support for parties in the alliance, including the Christian Democrats and the rightist People's Party, at around 22 percent.
The Liberal Democrats were backed by up to 23 percent of voters in recent surveys.

If called on to form a new government, Drnovsek will have to turn to one or two of the right-wing parties to help him push through further economic reforms amid growing calls from workers for higher pay.
